speaker: Tobias Lütke
title: Tobi Lütke: 21 Years of Building Shopify
question: In a scaling technology company, why do ad-hoc executive headcount requests quietly starve product innovation?
guest: We created a desired-state system for the company—a model of what the company should look like based on our agreed constraints, held up against what actually is. Think about how much politics this removes. When my head of sales comes to me and says, 'Hey, I need fifty new salespeople,' I can put this into the system and it says, 'Well, that means you have to either make these changes or you're going to lose some of your engineers,' because the system recomputes everything based on our agreements. So we can always look at the counterfactual. It's not like the boss agreed while playing golf to hire fifty more salespeople, and now someone has to carve a pound of flesh somewhere out of the engineering team, and suddenly you don't actually work on innovation anymore—because you never actually made the decision to stop hiring engineers, your budget just doesn't allow it anymore. Maybe hiring salespeople is the right decision, but now we can actually look at the consequences of every one of those choices.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Ad-hoc executive headcount requests starve innovation because they bypass the one moment when trade-offs are made explicit. Headcount is effectively a company's real strategy: where people sit determines what gets built. When an executive secures engineers through a hallway conversation or an escalation rather than through a planning process, the request is judged in isolation ("is this worth five people?") instead of comparatively ("is this worth more than what those five would otherwise do?"). Almost every individual request passes the first test.

The cost falls on whatever has the weakest advocate, which is usually exploratory product work. Urgent, legible needs such as a sales-driven feature, a compliance gap, or a pet initiative come with a sponsor and a deadline. Innovation bets have uncertain payoffs and no customer shouting for them, so their budget becomes the reserve everyone draws from.

The starvation is quiet because nothing is formally cancelled. Teams are simply left understaffed, backfills are redirected, and people are "borrowed" temporarily. Each exception also teaches leaders that lobbying beats planning, so the pattern compounds, and roadmaps drift towards short-term, incremental work.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: In a scaling technology company, ad-hoc executive headcount requests quietly starve product innovation by bypassing portfolio trade-offs and taxing existing engineering capacity. Because budgets and recruiting bandwidth are finite, off-cycle approvals treat each hire as an isolated exception rather than a zero-sum allocation, steadily draining the financial and hiring runway needed for long-term product bets without ever forcing an explicit roadmap cut. Reactive requests naturally favor urgent, easily defended operational pain, such as customer escalations, custom enterprise demands, or firefighting, over speculative innovation whose payoff is quarters away. Worse, unplanned hires are not free capacity: interviewing, onboarding, and integrating them pull senior engineers and product leaders away from discovery and core architecture. As those reactive roles solidify into permanent, fragmented teams that demand ongoing coordination, platform support, and maintenance, the company’s resources silently shift from creating new product value to sustaining organizational complexity.

noweb.answer: In a scaling technology company, ad-hoc executive headcount requests starve product innovation by redirecting finite capital, recruiting capacity, and senior attention toward urgent, politically backed fires. Because total budget and hiring bandwidth are rarely elastic, every unplanned role approved between planning cycles quietly delays or displaces hires intended for long-horizon research and development. Existing engineers and product leaders also absorb the hidden tax of interviewing, onboarding, and integrating these additions, pulling their focus away from deep, speculative building. Furthermore, off-cycle requests typically serve reactive needs, such as bespoke enterprise demands, operational patches, or isolated pet initiatives, rather than coherent architectural bets. Once onboarded, these hires create new workstreams, cross-functional coordination overhead, and maintenance obligations that core platform and product teams must support indefinitely. Because no single request appears to cancel a major initiative, the trade-off remains invisible. Over time, however, the company’s center of gravity shifts from compounding product breakthroughs to servicing fragmented commitments, starving innovation not through an explicit cut, but through the steady accumulation of unplanned obligations.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Ad-hoc executive headcount requests starve innovation because they bypass the planning process that weighs every role against strategic priorities. Requests from senior leaders tend to get approved on authority, urgency, or personal relationships, not on a comparison of expected returns. Each approval looks small and reasonable by itself. Together they draw down a fixed budget, and they usually go to functions that are already established or politically visible, such as sales coverage, operations backfills, or an executive's staff.

Innovation loses this contest for structural reasons. Exploratory product bets have uncertain, delayed payoffs and rarely have a powerful sponsor pushing for them mid-cycle. They're also the easiest line items to defer, because nothing visibly breaks when they go unfunded. Nobody decides to kill them. They just get pushed to the next planning cycle. Meanwhile, each ad-hoc hire adds fixed cost and coordination overhead that carries into future budgets, which shrinks the discretionary pool again.

The fix is to run headcount through a single portfolio process, protect a separate allocation for innovation, and make every exception show what it displaces.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Ad-hoc executive headcount requests starve product innovation because they quietly consume finite capital, recruiting bandwidth, and leadership attention without ever competing directly against the product roadmap. Each unplanned hire typically responds to an urgent, visible symptom—a major customer escalation, a sales gap, or an operational bottleneck—making it easy to justify in isolation. Because these approvals happen outside structured planning cycles, they bypass the trade-off discipline that forces leaders to weigh short-term relief against long-horizon bets.

Over time, the effect compounds. Every ad-hoc role locks in recurring fixed payroll, adds coordination overhead, and absorbs engineering and management capacity to onboard and integrate. Because no single request looks large enough to threaten strategy, the company rarely notices the shift until its discretionary R&D budget is gone. What remains is an organization staffed to service yesterday's friction rather than build tomorrow's capabilities, leaving product teams with neither the unallocated talent nor the runway required for genuine innovation.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Every executive headcount request can make sense on its own. The problem is that each approval commits part of a finite hiring budget without forcing a decision about which planned work will give way. Urgent requests usually have a senior sponsor and a visible deadline. Product experiments have uncertain returns, so delaying them is easier to justify.

The cost often shows up as a vacancy or a delay. A product team can have enough engineers on paper and still be unable to test a new idea because its designer or data scientist has been reassigned. The roadmap stays intact while teams run fewer experiments and learn more slowly. And because each hire adds recurring payroll, those one-off decisions leave less room to invest in new ideas in the next planning cycle, too.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Executive headcount requests often get considered one at a time. Each comes with a named sponsor and an immediate problem. A product idea still being tested has uncertain returns, and nobody has to say which experiment matters less when approving the hire.

Yet every approval commits recurring payroll and, while the company is scaling, consumes scarce recruiting and onboarding time. Product teams can keep their roadmap on paper while waiting months for the designer or engineer they need to test an idea. They protect customer commitments and deadlines by cutting the work that is easiest to postpone: discovery and experimentation.

The effect is quiet because no executive has to cancel innovation. A series of individually reasonable hiring decisions can leave the company with more employees and fewer opportunities to learn what it should build next.
